surprise.title: The hill behind FSU's 175th homecoming is the oldest college site in Florida
surprise.body: Florida State is celebrating 175 years this weekend because in 1851 the Florida Legislature voted to create two state seminaries, and the western one became today's university. The West Florida Seminary opened for classes in Tallahassee in 1857 on the old Florida Institute property, the exact spot where the Westcott Building stands now. That makes it the oldest continuously used site of higher education in the state, on ground that early Tallahassee knew by a darker name: Gallows Hill, where public executions once took place. The school wore several identities along the way. In 1905 the Buckman Act made it a women's college, known from 1909 as the Florida State College for Women, and after World War II it went coeducational again to absorb G.I. Bill students and took the name Florida State University. Westcott itself went up in 1910, Collegiate Gothic by architect William Augustus Edwards, which is why it photographs so well for grad portraits and anchored Grad Arena's first Instagram carousel. Today the Homecoming Parade steps off at 3:30 PM from the Tucker Civic Center, under a gray, mild sky in the mid-60s. Twenty-three days until you sail on December 13.
